title: A Blow to Voting Rights: Supreme Court Lets Stand Ruling That Bars Private Lawsuits in 7 States
summary: For decades, if a voter with a disability or limited English needed assistance at the polls, private groups could go to court to defend that right. That changed Monday when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review a lower-court ruling that eliminates the ability of private individuals and organizations to sue under Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act in seven states. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which covers Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota, had ruled last year that only the U.S. attorney general can bring lawsuits to enforce Section 208. That provision allows voters who are blind, have a disability, or cannot read or write to receive assistance from a person of their choice—except their employer or union. The case began when Arkansas United, an immigrant advocacy group, challenged an Arkansas law limiting how many voters a non-poll worker can assist. The group had provided Spanish-language interpreters at polling sites. A federal judge initially blocked the state law, but the appeals panel reversed, finding the group had no “private right of action.” The Supreme Court’s unsigned order offered no explanation, but Arkansas Republican officials had argued there was no conflict among appeals courts requiring review. Attorneys for Arkansas United countered that the 8th Circuit’s decision is an “anomaly” that breaks with decades of precedent. This is the latest in a series of setbacks for the Voting Rights Act. In May, the high court sidestepped a similar question on Section 2, which prohibits racial discrimination in redistricting, sending two cases back to lower courts. The legal uncertainty stems from a 2021 opinion by Justice Neil Gorsuch, who questioned whether private parties can sue under the act. Since then, Republican officials in multiple states have argued that only the Justice Department can enforce these provisions. Voting rights advocates warn that relying solely on the federal government—with its limited resources and shifting political priorities—will lead to a dramatic decline in enforcement. “The limited case law regarding private enforcement of Section 208 does not mean that the circuit split is nonexistent, or that the issue is unimportant,” MALDEF attorneys wrote. “Instead, it demonstrates just how much of an anomaly the Eighth Circuit's decision is.” For now, the 8th Circuit stands alone, but the door is open for other courts to follow.
why_it_matters: When the power to protect voting rights shifts from ordinary citizens and advocacy groups to only the federal government, the strength of enforcement can depend heavily on who holds the presidency and how many resources the Department of Justice can spare — meaning that the rights of voters with disabilities or limited English could become less secure depending on political winds.

background_read: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is a landmark US law that bans racial discrimination in voting. Section 208, added later, specifically guarantees that voters who are blind, have a disability, or cannot read or write may bring a helper of their choice into the voting booth.

Private enforcement—when ordinary citizens or groups sue to protect rights instead of waiting for the government—has been a key tool in civil rights law for generations. For the Voting Rights Act, courts have long assumed that private groups like the NAACP could sue under many of its provisions, but the Supreme Court has never definitively ruled on this question for Section 208.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in St. Louis, is one of 13 federal appeals courts. Its ruling is the first to say that only the U.S. attorney general can enforce Section 208, creating a split with what many lawyers understood the law to mean.

By declining to hear the case, the Supreme Court left the 8th Circuit’s decision in place for now without setting a nationwide rule. That means the door is open for other appeals courts to reach different conclusions, producing more legal uncertainty.

perspectives.perspective: Positive – states' rights and legal clarity
perspectives.description: Some state officials and legal scholars argue that private lawsuits can create a chaotic patchwork of enforcement and that it is more orderly for only the federal government to decide when to sue. They say this respects the traditional role of the attorney general as the nation's chief law officer and prevents courts from being flooded with claims.

Voting rights advocates see this as a major blow to the Voting Rights Act. Private groups have historically filled enforcement gaps when the federal government was unwilling or unable to act. With this ruling, vulnerable voters in seven states may have no practical way to defend their right to assistance if the Department of Justice lacks the resources or political will to sue.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical – an unresolved circuit split
perspectives.description: From a legal perspective, the Supreme Court's decision not to intervene now means that what one appeals court believes the law means may differ from what other courts believe. This fragmentation can create confusion and unequal rights depending on where a voter lives, eventually forcing the Supreme Court to settle the matter once the split deepens.

Advocates may try to bring a similar case in another circuit where courts are more favorable to private enforcement, hoping to create a direct split that the Supreme Court cannot ignore. Meanwhile, Congress could amend the Voting Rights Act to explicitly grant a private right of action, but such legislation would be fiercely debated.
